# sysutils_timezone (Resource)

Sets the system time zone: `/etc/localtime` becomes a symlink to the zone's file in `/usr/share/zoneinfo`, and `/etc/timezone` names the zone on distributions that use it (Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine). Uses `timedatectl` when systemd is PID 1 and the provider's `root_dir` is not set. There is one system time zone, so there must be at most one `sysutils_timezone` per host (or per `root_dir`). On destroy the zone stays as it is, unless `restore_on_destroy` is set.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Run the host on Berlin time. /etc/localtime becomes a symlink to
# /usr/share/zoneinfo/Europe/Berlin, and /etc/timezone names the zone on
# Debian, Ubuntu and Alpine.
resource "sysutils_timezone" "this" {
  timezone = "Europe/Berlin"
}

# Put back the previous time zone when the resource is destroyed, for
# example on a shared test machine.
# resource "sysutils_timezone" "this" {
#   timezone           = "UTC"
#   restore_on_destroy = true
# }
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `timezone` (String) IANA time zone name, such as `"Europe/Berlin"`, `"America/New_York"` or `"UTC"`. Components separated by `/` of letters, digits, `_`, `+` and `-`. When applying, `/usr/share/zoneinfo/<timezone>` must be a compiled zone file (inside the provider's `root_dir` if set), so tzdata must be installed.

### Optional

- `restore_on_destroy` (Boolean) Whether destroy puts back the `/etc/localtime` and `/etc/timezone` that were there before the resource was created. They are recorded in the resource's private state on create; after import there is nothing to restore, and destroy only warns. Defaults to `false`: destroy leaves the time zone as it is.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Always `"system"`.

## How the Zone Is Set

The zone must be installed: `/usr/share/zoneinfo/<timezone>` must be a compiled zone file (starting with `TZif`) when applying, which rules out typos and files such as `zone.tab`. Symlinks inside the zoneinfo tree, such as `UTC -> Etc/UTC` on Debian, are followed. Minimal container images often lack tzdata; install it first, for example with [`sysutils_package`](./package.md).

- **With systemd as PID 1 and without `root_dir`**, `timedatectl set-timezone` sets the zone, so that `systemd-timedated`, which keeps the zone in memory, reports the new one. If `timedatectl` fails, for example because D-Bus is not running, the provider sets `/etc/localtime` itself and reports the failure as a warning.
- **Otherwise**, including in containers and below the provider's [`root_dir`](../index.md#root-directory), `/etc/localtime` is replaced atomically with a symlink to `../usr/share/zoneinfo/<timezone>`: a new symlink is created under a temporary name and renamed over the old entry, which may be a symlink or a regular file (a copy of a zone file, as older installers make). A directory or other special file at `/etc/localtime` is refused. The relative target is what `systemd` writes; it also points to the right file when the tree below `root_dir` is looked at from the host.
- **`/etc/timezone`** is written with the zone name if it exists already, or if `/etc/debian_version` or `/etc/alpine-release` exists, since Debian, Ubuntu and Alpine tools read it. It is written atomically, keeping its mode, owner, ACLs and SELinux label; a missing one is created with mode `0644`. A symlink at `/etc/timezone` is refused.
- Nothing is written if the zone is already set, and edits of `/etc/localtime` and `/etc/timezone` are serialised with other resources of the provider.

Running programs pick up the new zone the next time they check `/etc/localtime`; glibc does so whenever a program formats a local time. Programs that cache the zone, such as long-running Java services, need a restart.

## Drift Detection

On refresh, the zone is read back from the symlink target of `/etc/localtime`, absolute or relative. The plan shows an update back to the configured zone if:

- `/etc/localtime` points to another zone, or somewhere outside `/usr/share/zoneinfo` (the target is shown as the current value);
- `/etc/localtime` is missing, or is a regular file that is not a copy of the zone named in `/etc/timezone`;
- `/etc/localtime` is right, but `/etc/timezone` names another zone.

A regular file at `/etc/localtime` that is a byte-for-byte copy of the zone named in `/etc/timezone` counts as that zone; it is replaced with a symlink the next time the zone changes.

## Destroy and `restore_on_destroy`

By default destroy leaves the time zone as it is: removing `/etc/localtime` would silently switch the host to UTC.

With `restore_on_destroy = true`, destroy puts back what was there when the resource was created. On create, before changing anything, the provider records `/etc/localtime` (its symlink target, its content if it was a regular file, or that it was missing) and the content of `/etc/timezone` in the resource's private state, which Terraform stores with the state but does not show. Destroy restores them exactly, including a relative or absolute symlink target, and removes an `/etc/timezone` that did not exist. If the previous zone was a symlink into `/usr/share/zoneinfo` and `timedatectl` is used for applying, it is set with `timedatectl` first.

An imported resource has no recorded previous zone; with `restore_on_destroy = true`, its destroy leaves the zone in place and warns.

## Import

There is one system time zone, so the import ID is always `system`:

```shell
# There is one system time zone, so the import ID is always "system".
terraform import sysutils_timezone.this system
```

Import reads the zone from `/etc/localtime` and fails if it does not select one in `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. `restore_on_destroy` is `false` after import.

## Caveats

- There is one time zone per host, or per `root_dir`. Two `sysutils_timezone` resources for the same host fight over it, and so do a `sysutils_timezone` and a [`sysutils_symlink`](./symlink.md) or [`sysutils_file`](./file.md) managing `/etc/localtime`.
- Only the zone is managed. Whether the hardware clock keeps local time or UTC (`timedatectl set-local-rtc`) and time synchronisation are left alone.
- Some distributions read the zone from elsewhere, such as `ZONE=` in `/etc/sysconfig/clock` on old RHEL releases or `/etc/conf.d/hwclock`; those files are not changed.
- The resource only works on Unix-like systems.
